answer:
**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you to finish college: don't drop out to start a startup at 20. Use college to learn powerful things. There's one exception. If a side project you're working on takes off without you forcing it, it may be reasonable to run with it.

**Based on:** said it (his 2014 Stanford lecture, and a 2026 essay that doesn't contradict it)

**Why he'd say it**
- He says it flatly: "Do not start a startup in college." He adds that "20 is not the optimal time to do it." ([Before the Startup, 2014 @ 18:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s))
- He thinks waiting costs you nothing: "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." He also says a startup takes over your life, and early success would take away the open-ended exploration your twenties are good for. (@ 21:12)
- His advice for college is "learn powerful things," because "the component of entrepreneurship … that really matters is domain expertise." ([@ 30:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1815s)) His 2026 essay says the same: "The hard part of startups is product," and that knowledge comes from fields like CS or biology ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)).
- His exception: if a side project takes off, "you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." ([@ 21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s)) In 2026 he leans harder on this. He points out that Microsoft and Meta were started during Harvard's reading period, and says that when a project takes off, the student has to either abandon it or drop out.

**What would change his answer:** You would need real evidence of traction: users actually pulling the product from you, not just an idea you're excited about. Then dropping out becomes a reasonable choice.

His 2026 essay is written to universities, not to students. It doesn't say outright whether you should drop out, only that you'd have to choose. So if you have an idea but no traction, his advice is to build it on the side while you're in school and see whether it takes off.

I've found the relevant pages in the vault. Here's the answer.

**Verdict:** Don't go out and pitch now. Spend the time making something users love and growing it until you hit a milestone people can see, then raise on that. But PG wouldn't tell you to wait for revenue for its own sake either: the milestone is what matters.

**Based on:** the vault has his view on how fundraising works, but no direct "raise now or bootstrap" question. The verdict applies that view to your case.

**Why he'd say it**
- Being able to show traction matters far more than pitching skill: "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning ... growing fast, and then simply tell investors so." ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 9:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s), 2014). Also: "Someone who knows zero about fund raising but has made something users really love will have an easier time raising money." (@ 13:17)
- Raise in stages, each one tied to a milestone: "So you just do what you can on the money you got. As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more." ([yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 12:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s), Sept 2026). He also says "I think you can still start a startup on not much money." (@ 11:37)
- Michael Seibel, a YC partner, learned this the hard way. Justin.tv spent about eight months failing to raise, then with two months of runway left the team decided "we got to figure out how to make this thing profitable or we're going to die." He says they got more done in those two months than in all the months of pitching ([yt-7TU636F_yVQ @ 6:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s)).

**What would change his answer:** If you're already a well-known expert in your field, you can raise on credibility alone. He gives the example of a founder who raised on a white paper and a booked launch date (yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 12:42). It also changes if what you're building can't reach a first milestone without outside money. Even then he'd have you raise only enough to get to the next stage.

PG's essays "Ramen Profitable" and "Default Alive or Default Dead?" fit this answer closely. Neither has been added to the vault yet, so I didn't quote them. Getting to "ramen profitable" means you can raise when you choose to rather than because you have to.

The vault covers this directly. PG gave a 2026 talk in Stockholm on exactly this question, so here's his answer.

**Verdict:** Move to San Francisco, at least for a while, and then come back to Berlin if you want to. PG says every field has one center and ambitious people should go to it. The main reasons are better peers, chance meetings and faster investors, and what being there does to your ambition.

**Based on:** he said it. His April 2026 Stockholm talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8) answers this question for a European audience.

**Why he'd say it**
- He gives a flat yes: "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([@ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s))
- **Peers and chance meetings.** "You get the best peers… The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." ([@ 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=69s)) He also says nothing beats "serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff" ([@ 3:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=200s)).
- **What it does to you.** "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." ([@ 8:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=499s)) Seeing the big winners up close makes the goal "hard" instead of "impossible".
- **Investors.** "Investors outside Silicon Valley implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate… if you leave for Silicon Valley, you make this rule operate in reverse." ([@ 6:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s))

**Coming back is fine, even good:** he says returning founders bring back Valley money and culture. He also says a European city could still become "the Silicon Valley of Europe. That job is still up for grabs." ([@ 20:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1204s)) His preferred way to do the trip is YC.

**What would change his answer:** almost nothing in the startup case. His one personal caveat is "Money isn't everything. Once you have kids, you'll find you care more about them than your company." ([@ 19:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1170s))

**Two cautions:**
- PG has a stake in this advice. He admits it himself: "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book."
- His claim that startups going home after YC are "half as likely to become unicorns" is YC's internal data, given without the underlying numbers or method. He discounts it himself for selection bias.

Sam Altman (July 2026) agrees but less firmly. He thinks moving to the Bay Area is probably still right but has "less of an intuition for it now."

**Verdict:** PG would say "pivot or persist" is the wrong question. Hold on to the goal and the problem, and give up the current approach once its expected value has clearly dropped. Your argument with your co-founder should be about which level the pivot is at, not about which of you is more stubborn.

**Based on:** follows from what they said. The vault has nothing from PG on co-founders disagreeing about a pivot, but his essay on persistence settles it.

**Why he'd say it**
- Persistence means sticking to the goal, not to your plan for reaching it: "The persistent are attached to the goal. The obstinate are attached to their ideas about how to reach it." ([The Right Kind of Stubborn](https://paulgraham.com/persistence.html))
- His deciding rule: "You'll give way on any point low down in the decision tree, if its expected value drops sufficiently, but energy and resilience keep pushing you toward whatever you chose higher up." He adds: "persistence often requires that one change one's mind."
- His test for which one you are is how you react when someone points out a problem. The Collisons "listen with an almost predatory intensity," and successful people are "never more engaged than when you disagree with them." Before you dig in, take your co-founder's case seriously.
- Seibel (YC) draws the same line: "hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely." ([How to Plan an MVP @ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s)). What he warns against is keeping the thing you built and hunting for a new problem it could solve.

**What would change his answer:** if your co-founder wants to drop the problem or the customer because the evidence says it's worth less than you thought, that's a change at the top of the tree. PG says it's fine to be "irrational near the top of the decision tree" and choose a problem you love. But then you're arguing about where you want to go, not about tactics, and you two have to settle that yourselves.

**Verdict:** Ship the tiny version this week. The vault doesn't have Paul Graham saying this himself, but it's YC's documented position, and it matches what PG wrote in essays that aren't in the vault.

**Based on:** Seibel and Caldwell said it (in the vault). PG's own view is beyond the vault.

There's a gap you should know about. The vault has 11 of PG's essays, and none of them cover when to launch. His only "launch" quote in the vault ("nothing is convincing as booking a launch") is about booking a rocket launch for a space startup, so it doesn't apply here. The launch material in the vault comes from Michael Seibel and Dalton Caldwell.

**Why they'd say it**
- Seibel calls it the one rule to remember: "if you can walk away from one thing from this presentation, it's launch something bad quickly." He adds that it has "been part of the YC ethos from the very beginning" ([yt-1hHMwLxN6EM @ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s)).
- A launch can be small: "How about launch is when you get any customers." Do that soon and leave the press launch for later ([@ 10:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=607s)).
- Building the full product first tells you nothing: "until you can put something in front of people, you have no faking idea whether it's going to work." ([@ 10:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=639s))
- The 2026 version of the advice is the same. Caldwell launched StandardDB with AI coding tools and said "I had to delete 80% of the features that I built in the MVP." ([yt-rQtrzBcf_Us @ 1:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQtrzBcf_Us&t=66s)) Cheap features make it easier to overbuild, so cutting matters more.

**PG himself (not in the vault):** He has written this many times, including "Release early" in *The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn* and "launch fast" in *Startups in 13 Sentences*. His argument is that you only find out what to build once users are using it.

**What would change their answer:** Seibel's one exception is heavily regulated fields like insurance or banking, where "it's harder to launch" ([@ 8:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=506s)).

To close the gap, you could add PG's launch essays to the vault: *The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn*, *Startups in 13 Sentences* and *Do Things that Don't Scale*.

**Verdict:** Start the startup now. PG tried the "work somewhere else for a few years first" advice, called it a mistake, and dropped it. The way to learn to start a startup is to try one.

**Based on:** said it (2014). His 2023 and 2026 writing points the same way.

**Why he'd say it**
- He took back this exact advice: "One of the things I got wrong early on, is that I advised people who were interested in starting a startup to go work for some other company for a few years before starting their own. But, honestly, the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it. You may not be successful, but you'll learn faster if you just do it." (Stanford CS183B, 2014 @ 33:36, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2016s)
- What a big company teaches doesn't help much at the start. Management "is a problem that you only have in a startup if you're sufficiently successful", and what you need early on is "developing products" (same talk @ 33:05). In 2026 he still says the hard part is product: knowing what to build and being able to build it.
- Risk is cheapest when you're young: "Ambitious people of two types: those who know they're so good that they'll be net ahead in a world with higher variation, and those, particularly the young, who can afford to risk trying it to find out." Also: "take multiple shots. Which is another reason to start taking risks early." (*Superlinear Returns*, 2023, https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)

**What would change his answer:** He also says the high-variance path "is not for everyone" and that "Most people will be better off as part of the pool." If what you want is the security of a job, Google is a fine choice. Just don't tell yourself it's startup training.

**Other YC voices:** Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel (2026) say that if you can't find an ambitious idea, you're better off working somewhere ambitious than spending years on a small one. So "no idea yet" is the one case where YC people do recommend taking a job.

**Beyond the vault:** PG's essays on big companies, like *You Weren't Meant to Have a Boss*, say the same thing. Those essays aren't in the vault, so I haven't quoted them.

**Verdict:** Go for the hard, ambitious idea, provided you actually find it interesting and you want a big outcome rather than just an income. PG doesn't give a flat yes or no here. His rule depends on your goal. If you just want to make money, work on what people pay for. If you want to get very rich or do great work, work on what interests you most, and the second case decides this one.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has no PG statement on "AI tool now vs. a hard idea later" specifically.

**Why he'd say it**
- He calls the money question a "midwit peak": "if you want to become super rich, and you're young and good at technology, working on what you're most interested in becomes a good idea again." For modest money, though, "People pay you for doing what they want, not what you want." ([When To Do What You Love](https://paulgraham.com/when.html))
- His best office-hours question is what would make a company more *powerful*, because asking how to make more money "tends to yield incremental improvements." He also says early founders often play it safe out of fear: "unconsciously cowering by doing something less ambitious than they could." ([powerful.html](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html))
- He doesn't think "might take years" means you need lots of money first: "even a rocket startup you can start on not much money because what you do is you adjust for how much money you've got." Reach a milestone, then raise again. ([interview @ 11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=697s))
- Interest is required, not optional: "The root of great work is a sort of ambitious curiosity, and you can't manufacture that." (when.html)

**What would change his answer:** if what you mainly want is reliable income, or the ambitious idea doesn't truly interest you, then by his own rule you should build the AI tool that pays.

The strongest "small ideas kill startups" argument in the vault comes from Seibel and Caldwell, not PG. They limit it to companies that raise venture money and say that if you really want a small business, you shouldn't raise VC.

**Verdict:** Focus on building. Paul Graham would see posting for attention as one of the startup "tricks", which matter far less than making something users love. He would still tell you to write, though, because for him writing is how you think, and an audience can compound over time. Writing is something to do alongside building, not instead of it.

**Based on:** follows from what they said. The vault has no essay or talk where PG directly answers "should founders blog?"

**Why they'd say it**
- In his 2014 "Before the Startup" talk, he says what makes or breaks a startup is the product: "There are tricks in the startups, as there are in any domain. But they are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem. Someone who knows zero about fund raising but has made something users really love will have an easier time raising money. Than someone who knows every trick in the book, but has a flat usage graph." ([talk @ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s))
- He values writing as thinking, not as marketing: "writing is thinking. In fact there's a kind of thinking that can only be done by writing." ([Writes and Write-Nots, 2024](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html)) Writing to get your ideas about users and the market straight is part of building.
- He counts an audience as work that compounds: work compounds "when you're building infrastructure, or growing an audience or brand." ([Superlinear Returns, 2023](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)) Once the product is working, a slowly growing audience is a reasonable side investment.
- Sam Altman, another YC voice, warns specifically about Twitter: "you should like put all of your energy into building stuff and like resist the easy shots." ([talk @ 22:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1348s))

**What they've done:** PG wrote essays mostly after Viaweb, not while he was running it. Those essays and his talks then helped launch YC (not in the vault).

**What would change their answer:** If writing is itself how you reach users, for example a developer tool whose users read your posts, then writing counts as building.

**Verdict:** PG would tell you to stay small. Raising the seed doesn't mean it's time to hire. Ideally you've already found success before you hire even two or three people, and the money is for reaching the next milestone, not for building a team.

**Based on:** something he said directly (2014, early hires), plus his principles applied to your case. The strongest version of this view is in his essays, which aren't in the vault.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Wait to hire.** "ideally, you're successful before you even hire two or three people… Airbnb took five months to hire their first employee… ideally, you don't have even two or three people for quite a while." ([2014 lecture](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2084s) @ 34:44)
- **Early hires are almost founders.** "the first hires in a startup are almost like founders… You shouldn't have to manage them much." He also says management is "a problem that you only have in a startup if you're sufficiently successful." (same lecture @ 34:44, 35:18, 33:05). If your hires would need managing, you're hiring too early.
- **Spend to milestones.** "you just do what you can on the money you got. As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more." ([Sept 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s) @ 12:09). A big team shortens your runway without obviously getting you to the milestone sooner.
- **AI hasn't changed this.** "so far almost everything is exactly the same." The bottleneck is still how fast you ship, and that depends on thinking up the ideas, not on how many people are producing ([Sept 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=964s) @ 16:04–16:38).

**From his essays (not in the vault):** In "Default Alive or Default Dead" (2015) and "Startups in 13 Sentences" he calls hiring too fast one of the most common ways funded startups die. You raise, you hire to look like a "real" company, the burn rate jumps, and you end up default dead.

**What would change his answer:** Users are already pulling the product out of your hands, and the founders can't keep up. Even then he'd want self-motivated peers you know and like, not people you have to manage. Livingston makes the same "start small" point from YC's own history ([2018](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1510s) @ 25:10).

If you do hire, Caldwell and Seibel (October 2026) say to treat it like sales and build a real pipeline. That's covered in `wiki/hiring/recruiting/winning-at-hiring.md`.

**Verdict:** Go with the one you're passionate about, as long as you're building a startup to go big, or you don't need much money. PG doesn't think early market size is worth worrying about. He does think real interest is what produces the huge outcomes.

**Based on:** said it (with one condition he sets himself)

**Why he'd say it**
- He calls this a "midwit peak." If you just want a good income, you usually work on what pays. But "if you want to become super rich, and you're young and good at technology, working on what you're most interested in becomes a good idea again." That's because the biggest startups began as projects done for fun ([When To Do What You Love, 2024](https://paulgraham.com/when.html)).
- On market size: "Don't worry about the second number, the market size. Since you predict future demand, the market will grow." He adds: "it's always possible to expand into adjacent markets. All you need is a beachhead" ([How to Earn a Billion Dollars, 2026](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html)).
- If you feel stuck between the two, he says that's "almost always due to ignorance." His fix is to "get more certainty," and the best way to do that is to "try working on things you're interested in" (When To Do What You Love).
- Market estimates made at the start tend to be too small. Seibel and Caldwell point out that Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe all turned out much bigger than their founders expected.

**What would change his answer:** if your passion is something few people want. "People pay you for doing what they want, not what you want." His market-size advice assumes you're building what you and people like you actually want, so you're predicting where demand is going. If your goal is a steady income rather than a huge outcome, he'd say follow the money.

One check he suggests for whether you're really interested: if the work didn't pay, would you take a day job and do it in your spare time?

**Verdict:** Apply to YC. PG would say the YC acceptance itself does a lot of the angel raising for you. Either way, the thing that actually gets you funded is a startup that's growing, not how you pitch it.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. Nothing in the vault has PG comparing "YC vs. raising from angels" head-on. His stated principles point clearly one way, though.

**Why he'd say it**
- Getting into YC changes how investors see you: "As soon as you tell them that you've been accepted by Y Combinator, often they're suddenly... they're tripping over themselves to try and invest in you" ([yt-QHJkUw31YX8 @ 6:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s)). He also says investors outside the Valley "implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate" (same talk), so this matters more if you're not in the Bay Area.
- He calls YC the best version of the Valley: "Surely the optimal way to go to Silicon Valley for a bit and then come back is to do YC" ([@ 17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s)).
- You'd get things a cheque from an angel doesn't come with. Founding a startup "is normally a very lonely business", and in a batch you get colleagues, peers who've already solved your technical problem, and batchmates as fast-deciding first customers ([yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 17:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=1031s)).
- The deciding factor is traction, not which route you pick: "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well... and then simply tell investors so" ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 9:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s)).

**What would change his answer:** if you're already growing fast enough that angels are chasing you, his "be doing well and say so" rule means you can raise without YC. Even then he'd point to the batch and the network as reasons to go.

**Discount for:** he's YC's co-founder, and he says so himself: "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book at this point" (@ 17:16). The vault doesn't cover YC's terms or how much equity it takes, so I haven't weighed dilution against an angel round.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you to find a co-founder, but not by searching for one. Start building now, alongside people you already know and like. The co-founder usually comes out of working on projects together.

**Based on:** mostly follows from what he said. Nothing in the vault has PG answering "solo or co-founder?" directly. His blunt answer to that comes from an essay that isn't in the vault (see the last bullet).

**Why he'd say it**
- You find out who's a good co-founder by working with them, not by interviewing them: "the only way to tell for sure if someone will be good to work with is to work with them. Apple and Microsoft were just the last of many projects their founders had worked on together." ([prepare.html](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html), 2026)
- So don't wait for a co-founder before you start. When you work on side projects at the leading edge, "that third part incidentally is how you get co-founders at the same time as the idea." ([Stanford 2014 @ 25:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1541s))
- Choose co-founders the way you choose friends: "people you genuinely like and respect ... and that you have known long enough to be sure." ([@ 4:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=278s)) Teaming up with a stranger just to have a co-founder goes against this.
- *(not in the vault)* In "The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups" (2006), PG lists **having a single founder as mistake #1**. His reasons: startups are too hard for one person, you need colleagues to bounce ideas off and to keep up morale, and a founder who couldn't persuade even one friend to join is a bad sign.

**What the other YC partners add:** Caldwell and Seibel (2026) say the most common way founders fail is losing hope and quitting, and that's harder to avoid alone. The solo founders they've seen succeed all "created co-founder-like ... environments and relationships that did fill the void" ([@ 3:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=194s)). Altman: "it's also very hard to do a startup on your own and very lonely."

**What would change the answer:** Caldwell allows that "not having a co-founder is fine for a lot of people" ([@ 2:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=131s)). Garry Tan (2026) argues that AI agents let one founder work like a whole organization. But no one in the vault says that replaces having a co-founder.

So, in practice: don't put off building to go co-founder hunting, and don't stay solo on purpose. Build in public, among people you already know. Whoever keeps showing up to work with you is probably your co-founder.
